For each $x\in[0,1)$, we have $x^n\to0$, while $f_n(1)=1$ for every $n$. Thus $(f_n)$ converges pointwise to the function
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x=1.\end{cases}
\]
Suppose that $(f_n)$ converges uniformly to some function $g$. Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence, so uniqueness of pointwise limits gives $g=f$. Taking $\varepsilon=\tfrac12$, uniform convergence would yield an integer $N\ge1$ such that $|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\tfrac12$ for every $n\ge N$ and every $x\in[0,1]$. Set $x=2^{-1/N}<1$. Then $f(x)=0$ and
\[
|f_N(x)-f(x)|=x^N=\tfrac12,
\]
a contradiction. Hence $(f_n)$ does not converge uniformly on $[0,1]$.
\end{proof}", "claim": "The sequence $f_n(x)=x^n$ has pointwise limit $f=0$ on $[0,1)$ and $f(1)=1$, and a fixed epsilon witness contradicts uniform convergence to this necessarily unique pointwise limit.", "depends_on": [], "scope": [], "goal_refs": ["main"]}], "target_dependencies_after": [], "counterexample": null, "reason": "This replacement defines and proves the pointwise limit, justifies that any uniform limit must equal it, and supplies a valid contradiction to the uniform convergence criterion."}, "patch_digest": "e9088bffeb9402f89f850a501bd3972e5fa66daf02ad0fd1f07139431b396c36", "certificate": {"certificate_id": "01a2ca499fe9955c42bccb0a28d2462f4f84d914c10ae2b9362620a209d0706f", "problem_digest": "e5fcea369deb30b6c131db77aba1a1b879c1171eb489f4427aebc25df4006bda", "target": {"node_id": "n1", "version": 1}, "graph_digest": "f3a81a2e3a747f8279d21714c96e9cb9de277cefd4217f80da7c793d30ee492e", "confirmation": "confirmed", "kind": "gap", "failed_edge": "The inference from the asserted equality involving an undefined function f to the conclusion that (f_n) has no uniform limit is incomplete.", "quote": "The sequence $\left(f_n\right)_n$ does not converge uniformly, since given $0<\varepsilon<1$ and $N \in \mathbb{Z}_{+}$, for $x=\varepsilon^{1 / N}$ we have $d\left(f_N(x), f(x)\right)=\varepsilon$.", "reason": "The function $f$ has not been defined or shown to be the pointwise limit. One must establish that $f_n(x)\to f(x)$ where $f(x)=0$ for $0\le x<1$ and $f(1)=1$, and that any uniform limit must equal this pointwise limit. Then, fixing for example $\varepsilon=1/2$, for every $N$ the choice $x=(1/2)^{1/N}<1$ gives $|f_N(x)-f(x)|=1/2$, contradicting uniform convergence."}, "proposed_proof": "\begin{proof}
For each $x\in[0,1)$, we have $x^n\to0$, while $f_n(1)=1$ for every $n$. Thus $(f_n)$ converges pointwise to the function
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x=1.\end{cases}
\]
Suppose that $(f_n)$ converges uniformly to some function $g$. Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence, so uniqueness of pointwise limits gives $g=f$. Taking $\varepsilon=\tfrac12$, uniform convergence would yield an integer $N\ge1$ such that $|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\tfrac12$ for every $n\ge N$ and every $x\in[0,1]$. Set $x=2^{-1/N}<1$. Then $f(x)=0$ and
\[
|f_N(x)-f(x)|=x^N=\tfrac12,
\]
a contradiction. Hence $(f_n)$ does not converge uniformly on $[0,1]$.
\end{proof}
 We can also apply Theorem 21.6: the convergence is not uniform since $f$ is not continuous.

\end{proof}"}
